label: What a security awareness programme has to cover, and why each topic is listed

mentor.diagnosis: You treated awareness training as one block of content about phishing. The objectives enumerate distinct topics because each addresses a behaviour that technical controls cannot reach.
contrast: Topic
The behaviour it targets
Why a control cannot do it instead
Policy handbooks
Knowing what is expected and acknowledging it
You cannot enforce a rule nobody has read
Password management
Reuse, sharing, weak choices, manager adoption
Policy sets limits; habits decide what happens inside them
Social engineering awareness
Being manipulated by urgency and authority
No filter catches a persuasive phone call
Removable media and cables
Plugging in found or gifted hardware
Port control helps; people still carry things in
Operational security
What staff disclose publicly about systems and roles
Nothing technical stops an informative conference talk
Situational awareness
Noticing tailgating, shoulder surfing, an unfamiliar face
Cameras record it; people have to act on it
Hybrid and remote work
Home networks, shared spaces, personal devices
The perimeter does not extend to a kitchen table
Insider threat awareness
Recognising and reporting concerning behaviour in colleagues
Monitoring sees actions, not the context around them
mentor.rule: Awareness exists for the part of the attack surface that is a person making a decision. If the stem describes a judgement call rather than a configuration, the answer is a training topic.
mentor.tell: A control already exists and was bypassed by someone doing something reasonable-seeming.
mentor.trap: Hybrid and remote work is listed in its own right. Training written for an office assumes a perimeter, a physical security posture and a network that remote staff do not have.
